lead: A call centre gets calls at a steady average rate. A component fails at a steady average rate. The exponential distribution is the model for the wait until the next such event when the rate stays constant and the past tells you nothing. One number, the rate λ, gives the whole curve: the density, the mean, the tail and the memoryless rule. It is the standard model for lifetimes, interarrival waits and decay times, and it is the continuous cousin of the geometric distribution.
prereq: You need Unit 2 (continuous random variables, pdf, CDF, conditional probability) and the discrete waiting model in Chapter 3.3.

sections.h3: The model: waiting at a constant rate

blocks.text: Events arrive one at a time at a constant average rate: a call reaches a helpline, a component fails, a nucleus decays. Let λ (lambda, a positive number) be that rate in events per unit time. Let T be the wait from now until the next event. T is continuous, and its distribution is the exponential.

blocks.where: λ > 0 is the rate in events per unit time; t is elapsed time in the same unit; e ≈ 2.71828 is the base of natural logs.

blocks.text: The density starts at height λ at t = 0 and falls smoothly. Short waits are common, long waits are rare but never impossible. Doubling λ halves every typical wait.

blocks.where: E[T] is the mean wait in time units; Var(T) is the variance in squared time units; SD(T) is the standard deviation.

blocks.text: The mean and the standard deviation are equal. A server component with mean life 2 years has λ = 1/2 = 0.5 per year, and its SD is also 2 years.
The exponential counts down in continuous time; the geometric distribution does the same job in whole trials. The count of events in a fixed interval is Poisson, covered in Chapter 3.2.

blocks.where: F is the CDF, the chance the event has happened by time t; S is the survival function, the chance it has not happened by time t; both are probabilities between 0 and 1.

blocks.text: With λ = 0.5 per year, P(T > 3) = e^(−1.5) = 0.2231, so P(T ≤ 3) = 1 − 0.2231 = 0.7769. The median m solves e^(−0.5m) = 0.5, giving m = ln 2 / 0.5 = 1.386 years: half of all components fail before that age.

The ratio h(t) = f(t)/S(t) is the hazard rate, the failure risk at time t given survival so far. For the exponential, h(t) = λe^(−λt) / e^(−λt) = λ, a constant. Among continuous lifetime models, only the exponential has a flat hazard; a few syllabi make this the defining property.

Suppose the component has already run for s years and is still working. The remaining wait T − s has exactly the same exponential distribution as a brand-new component. The distribution forgets the s years already spent.
P(T > s + t | T > s) = P(T > t) for all s ≥ 0, t ≥ 0
blocks.where: T is the exponential lifetime; s is the time already survived; t is the further time asked about; | means given that.

items: Write the conditional probability as a ratio: P(T > s + t | T > s) = P(T > s + t and T > s) / P(T > s).
Since s + t > s, the event {T > s + t} sits inside {T > s}, so the numerator is just P(T > s + t).
Put in the survival form: e^(−λ(s+t)) / e^(−λs).
Subtract the exponents: e^(−λs − λt + λs) = e^(−λt) = P(T > t).

blocks.text: Numbers with λ = 0.5 per year, s = 3, t = 2: e^(−2.5) / e^(−1.5) = e^(−1) = 0.3679, which is exactly P(T > 2). The 3 years already used add nothing to the risk.

The uniform distribution does not do this. If a bus is equally likely to come at any moment in the next 10 minutes, waiting 9 minutes leaves only 1 minute on average, not 5. The exponential forgets; the uniform remembers.
Two consequences for exams. Old working parts and new parts have the same remaining lifetime distribution. And P(T > 5 | T > 3) is not P(T > 5); it is P(T > 2).

figure.caption: How the exponential tail and the memoryless rule join up: the chance of lasting past 3 years, the rule that drops those 3 years, and the fresh 2-year wait that gives the same probability.

spec.title: Exponential memoryless check
spec.aria: Flow from an exponential lifetime with mean two years to a survival probability and the memoryless conditional equality.

examples.question: The lifetime T, in years, of a server component is exponential with mean 2 years. (a) Find P(T > 3). (b) Find P(T > 5 | T > 3). (c) Find the median lifetime.
steps: Convert the mean to the rate: λ = 1/mean = 1/2 = 0.5 per year.
(b) By memorylessness with s = 3 and t = 2: P(T > 5 | T > 3) = P(T > 2) = e^(−0.5 × 2) = e^(−1) = 0.3679. Check directly: e^(−2.5) / e^(−1.5) = e^(−1) = 0.3679.
examples.answer: P(T > 3) = 0.2231, P(T > 5 | T > 3) = 0.3679, and the median lifetime is 1.3863 years.
examples.check:
import math
lam = 1 / 2
p3 = math.exp(-lam * 3)
p5_given_3 = math.exp(-lam * 5) / math.exp(-lam * 3)
median = math.log(2) / lam
print(round(p3, 4))
print(round(p5_given_3, 4))
print(round(median, 4))

traps: Using the mean where the rate belongs. For mean 2 years, λ = 0.5, not 2; writing e^(−3) instead of e^(−1.5) is the classic slip.
Memoryless does not mean P(T > 5 | T > 3) = P(T > 5). It equals P(T > 2), the wait for the next 2 years only.
Writing the survival as 1 − e^(−λt). That is the CDF. The tail is e^(−λt) alone.
Mixing the geometric and the exponential. Geometric counts whole trials with qⁿ; exponential measures continuous time with e^(−λt).
Losing the time unit. A rate of 0.5 per year becomes 1/24 per month, so state λ in the same unit as t before substituting.

quiz.q: Write the pdf, mean and variance of the exponential distribution with rate λ.
quiz.a: f(t) = λe^(−λt) for t ≥ 0 and 0 otherwise; E[T] = 1/λ; Var(T) = 1/λ².

quiz.q: Why does the mean have to be 1/λ rather than λ?
quiz.a: λ is a count per unit time: a rate. The mean of T is a time, so it must be time per event, which is the reciprocal 1/λ. If λ doubles, waits halve.

quiz.q: T is exponential with λ = 0.25 per hour. Find P(T > 8).
A component's lifetime is exponential and P(T > 4) = 0.2. Find λ and the mean lifetime.
quiz.a: e^(−4λ) = 0.2, so −4λ = ln 0.2 = −1.6094, giving λ = 0.4024 per unit time. Mean = 1/λ = 2.4853 time units.

quiz.q: Prove that the exponential is memoryless, and show with a counterexample that the uniform on [0, 10] is not.
quiz.a: Proof: P(T > s + t | T > s) = e^(−λ(s+t)) / e^(−λs) = e^(−λt) = P(T > t). For U uniform on [0, 10], P(U > 9 | U > 6) = (1/10)/(4/10) = 0.25, but P(U > 3) = 0.7. The two differ, so the uniform remembers.

quiz.q: Which discrete distribution plays the role of the exponential, and in what way do they differ?
quiz.a: The geometric distribution. It counts whole trials until the first success with qⁿ, while the exponential measures continuous time with e^(−λt). Both are memoryless.

quiz.q: Why does a constant hazard rate force the memoryless property?
quiz.a: With h(t) = λ fixed, the risk of failing in the next instant does not depend on age. The survival then satisfies S(s + t) = S(s)S(t), which is exactly the memoryless statement.

quiz.q: Calls arrive at a mean gap of 5 minutes, exponential. A call just arrived. Find the chance the next one is more than 10 minutes away, and the same chance given 4 minutes have already passed.
quiz.a: λ = 1/5 per minute. P(T > 10) = e^(−2) = 0.1353. Given 4 minutes already passed, P(T > 14 | T > 4) = P(T > 10) = 0.1353, the same number.

beyond: Not for the exam. Reliability engineers use the exponential as the flat-hazard baseline and move to the Weibull when wear-out makes the hazard rise. Survival analysis in medicine uses the same survival function S(t) and hazard h(t), with the Cox model letting the hazard depend on patient covariates. Queueing theory builds on exponential interarrival and service times to get tractable formulas. Search next for hazard function, Weibull distribution and Cox proportional hazards.
